Lycoperdon (pedunculated) with a long stalk, globular head glabrous: mouth cylindrical, entirest. LIN. Sp. Plant.
1654.
It is very common in the lands of our Peninsula in the enclosures
of the marshy meadows, and I have also seen it in those of some orchards and gardens, and particularly in those of the Royal Site of Aranjuez,
and in others.
LYCOPERSICON. TOURNEFORT. Class II.
It is a genus of plant with a monopetalous flower, round, and divided into
many parts, from whose calyx emerges the pistil attached like a nail in the middle of the flower, which later becomes a soft, fleshy, and somewhat round fruit, divided into many cells full of seeds, usually flat.
I.
LYCOPERSICON Galeni. T. Inst. R. H. 150.
Solanum (Lycopersicon) with an unarmed herbaceous stem
CCC
leaves
9
OF THE
pinnate incised, simple racemes. LIN. SP. Plant. 265.
Officin. Apples of love. Castell. TOMATES.
It is cultivated in great abundance in the orchards and irrigated fields in all the Provinces and lands of our Peninsula, it is of great supply, and is sown every year. It flowers in March and April
in Andalusia, Murcia, and Valencia: so that in these Provinces
almost all year they enjoy the fruit even in winter, and I am witness
to having eaten them fresh, and freshly picked from the plant in the month of
January and February.
DESCRIPTION.
It consists of a white root, moderately thick and
fibrous
from it sprout shoots usually four, five, or more
feet long, hairy
, weak, hollow inside, branched, and covered with many cut leaves, with little difference like those of the
Agrimonia, toothed on the edges, pointed, tender, somewhat hairy, and of pale green color. The flowers arise between nipples, each having a node near the flower: these are supported by the
calyx cut into five parts:
the fruit is the size of a small apple, almost red, soft, and shiny, of pleasant taste,
and divided internally into several cells, which enclose many flat, and somewhat yellow seeds.
Most of the ancient Authors, and some modern ones,
especially the Northern ones, do not yet agree on the
virtues of the
Tomato; on the contrary, they are of the opinion that it should be placed
in the number of poisonous plants, rather than in the number of medicinal ones; but experience in our Peninsula teaches the exact opposite
and although in Italy, and particularly in Naples, they eat it dressed in salad
among us it has no comparison
with another vegetable on sumptuous and delicate tables all the time
that they last, seasoning the most delicious dishes, and forming the delicate sauce, which gives a pleasant flavor to the stew and other dishes.

tiernas para comerlas en ensalada como los pepinos. BELONIO refiere , que
en Egipto las cuecen en las cenizas calientes , ó en agua , y les sirven diariamente en las mesas ; pero se debe aconsejar que no se haga
abuso de ellas ; esto es , que no se coman con exceso , por convenir todos
los Autores en que es alimento , no solamente frio , é insípido , sino tambien perjudicial
á los sugetos de estómago endeble y delicado.
II.
MELONGENA fructu incurvo. T. Inst. R. H. 152.
Se diferencia de la anterior
solo
en que el
fruto es corvo , gozando en algo
la figura
de pepino , de color amarillo ceniciento , ó
purpureo , y se cultiva de continuo como la precedente en las huertas.
III.
MELONGENA fructu rotundo. T. Inst. R. H. 151 .
Esta Berengena se cria , y cultiva en las huertas y campos de regadío en Cataluña , lo mismo que las dos primeras , y
tiene las mismas qualidades y usos que la precedente.
IV.
MELONGENA fructu rotundo cum spinis violaceis.
T. Inst.
R. H. 152.
Solanum pomiferum , fructu rotundo spinis violaceis. H.
Lugd. Bat. 573.
Esta calidad de Berengena se cultiva en
las huertas de Madrid,
y es la que usan en
los guisados con los demas comestibles.
V.
MELONGENA fructu oblongo , albo . T. Inst. R. H. 151 .

The greatest medical use of the fruit is externally, and it enters
into
anodine and resolving cataplasms, for
cancers, burns,
inflammations and hemorrhoids. The internal use is not harmful, being used both in our Peninsula with foodstuffs; moreover the
inhabitants
of the Antilles cook the Eggplants removing the
skin,
afterwards they
cut them into four parts, and
eat them with oil and pepper. In our Spain they pickle them with vinegar when they are
tender to eat them in salad like cucumbers. BELONIO relates, that
in Egypt they cook them in hot ashes, or in water, and they serve them daily on the tables; but it should be advised that no
abuse be made of them; that is, that they not be eaten in excess, since all
Authors agree that it is food, not only cold and insipid, but also harmful
to subjects of weak and delicate stomach.
II.
MELONGENA with curved fruit. T. Inst. R. H. 152.
It differs from the previous one
only
in that the
fruit is curved, enjoying somewhat
the figure
of a cucumber, of ashen yellow color, or
purpureous, and it is continuously cultivated like the preceding one in gardens.
III.
MELONGENA with round fruit. T. Inst. R. H. 151 .
This Eggplant is grown, and cultivated in gardens and irrigated fields in Catalonia, just like the first two, and
has the same qualities and uses as the preceding one.
IV.
MELONGENA with round fruit with violet spines.
T. Inst.
R. H. 152.
Solanum pomiferum, with round fruit with violet spines. H.
Lugd. Bat. 573.
This quality of Eggplant is cultivated in
gardens of Madrid,
and is the one used in
stews with other foodstuffs.
